summary.text: Metamorphosis is a biological process in which an animal goes through a conspicuous and relatively abrupt change in body structure as part of its development.
It occurs in some insects, fish, amphibians and other groups, and can be complete, incomplete or absent depending on the species.
In insects, hormones from glands near the front of the body control it, and juvenile hormone prevents adult characteristics from developing.

facts.label: Complete type
facts.value: Holometaboly, with a pupal stage between larva and adult

facts.label: Incomplete type
facts.value: Hemimetaboly, where young nymphs resemble smaller wingless adults

facts.label: No metamorphosis
facts.value: Ametaboly, seen in bristletails and silverfish

facts.label: Flatfish change
facts.value: One eye moves to join the other on one side

facts.label: Fish control
facts.value: Thyroid hormone strongly controls fish metamorphosis

items.prompt: A caterpillar builds a chrysalis and later emerges as a butterfly. What kind of metamorphosis is this?

options.label: Complete, with an inactive pupal stage
Incomplete, with several nymph stages
None, since the animal develops directly
Only a change of diet, not of body

items.explain: Insects with complete metamorphosis pass through a larval stage, then an inactive pupa (chrysalis in butterflies), and finally emerge as adults.

items.prompt: A young grasshopper looks like a smaller, wingless adult and molts several times, growing wing buds. What type of development is this?

options.label: Complete metamorphosis through a pupa
Incomplete metamorphosis through nymph stages
Direct development with no change in form
A change of lifestyle with no body change

items.explain: Grasshoppers are hemimetabolous; their immature nymphs resemble adults, and wing buds form in later instars.

items.prompt: A hormone prevents adult features from developing during an insect's molts. In a holometabolous insect's final molt into an adult, how much of it is present?

options.label: A very high level
A low level
None at all
A steadily rising level

items.explain: Juvenile hormone is high in molts between larval instars, low at the molt to the pupa, and absent at the final molt.

items.prompt: In an insect, which part first releases the hormone that starts the chain leading to molting?

options.label: The prothoracic glands
The corpora allata
The old exoskeleton
Neurosecretory cells in the brain

items.explain: Neurosecretory cells in the brain secrete PTTH, which activates the prothoracic glands and also stimulates the corpora allata.

items.prompt: Many flatfish begin life with an eye on each side of the body. What happens as they become adults?

options.label: One eye moves to join the other on the upper side
Both eyes close and disappear
Both eyes move to the underside
A third eye forms on top of the head

items.explain: Flatfish start out bilaterally symmetrical, but one eye moves to join the other side, which becomes the upper side.

items.prompt: Hornworm caterpillars were trained to avoid an odour during their final larval stage. What happened after they became moths?

options.label: They forgot it, since the body is fully rebuilt
They still avoided that odour as adults
They were drawn to the odour instead
They stopped reacting to all odours

items.explain: The caterpillars continued to avoid the odour as adult moths after metamorphosis.

paragraphs.heading: A sudden change of body
paragraphs.text: Metamorphosis is a clear and fairly abrupt change in an animal's body structure that happens as part of its development. The word comes from Ancient Greek for "transformation", built from meta-, meaning "after", and morphe, meaning "form". Animals that have larval stages go through metamorphosis to reach the adult stage. It is found in some members of many animal groups, from insects, fish and amphibians to mollusks, crustaceans, cnidarians, echinoderms and tunicates, and it often comes with a change in nutrition or behavior.

paragraphs.heading: Three kinds
paragraphs.text: Complete metamorphosis, or holometaboly, joins life stages that look radically different. Incomplete metamorphosis, or hemimetaboly, joins stages that are somewhat alike, and some animals have no metamorphosis at all, called ametaboly. Insects show all three. In ametabolous insects the young barely differ from the adults, which is also called direct development. The earliest insects grew up this direct way, and some early ametabolous insects are still around, such as bristletails and silverfish.

paragraphs.heading: Incomplete metamorphosis
paragraphs.text: In hemimetabolous insects the young are called nymphs. They develop through repeated rounds of growth and moulting, or ecdysis, which means shedding the exoskeleton, and each of these stages is called an instar. Nymphs look a lot like adults, only smaller and missing wings, genitalia and other adult features. From one instar to the next the changes are small, and in later instars wing buds form on the outside. Cockroaches, grasshoppers, dragonflies and true bugs develop this way.

paragraphs.heading: Complete metamorphosis
paragraphs.text: In holometabolous insects the young are called larvae, and they differ markedly from the adults. After the larval stage they enter an inactive stage called the pupa, known in butterflies as a chrysalis, and then emerge as adults. Some learning survives the change. In a 2008 study, tobacco hornworm caterpillars trained to avoid a certain smell during their last larval stage still avoided it as adult moths.

paragraphs.heading: Hormones in charge
paragraphs.text: In insects, growth and metamorphosis are run by hormones made by glands near the front of the body. Neurosecretory cells in the brain release prothoracicotropic hormone (PTTH), which switches on the prothoracic glands. These release a second hormone, usually ecdysone, that sets off moulting. PTTH also prompts the corpora allata to make juvenile hormone, which keeps adult features from developing during a moult. In holometabolous insects, juvenile hormone is high in moults between larval stages, low in the moult to the pupa, and absent in the final moult to the adult.

paragraphs.heading: Fish and amphibians
paragraphs.text: In chordates, metamorphosis is induced by iodothyronines, and in fish it is usually under strong control by thyroid hormone. Many flatfish start life symmetrical, with one eye on each side, but one eye travels over so both sit on the side that becomes the top. Frogs, toads and newts hatch from eggs laid in water as larvae with external gills, and only later breathe with lungs. Newt larvae then hunt prey, while tadpoles mostly scrape food off surfaces using horny tooth ridges.
